```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(apa7)
```

The apa7 package makes tables in the style of the *Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association* (7th edition). Most of its functions take a fitted model or a data frame and return a finished table: regression coefficients, ANOVA source tables, descriptive statistics, correlations, reliability, factor loadings, marginal means, meta-analyses, and more. It also has functions for formatting numbers and statistics in APA style, in tables and in text.

apa7 builds its tables with the [flextable](https://ardata-fr.github.io/flextable-book/) package, which has the fullest support for Word (.docx) documents, so the tables look right in Word, HTML, and PDF. It works in [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) and R Markdown documents, and with [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/), a Quarto extension for writing whole papers in APA style.

```{r}
#| label: setup2
#| eval: false
library(apa7)
```

# Example: Report a Regression Analysis

The `sat.act` data set in the psych package has the self-reported ACT and SAT scores of 700 people. Give the variables names that will read well in a table, and keep the people with all of their scores:

```{r}
#| label: data
d_sat <- psych::sat.act |>
  na.omit() |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Gender = factor(gender, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    Age = age,
    ACT,
    Verbal = SATV,
    Quantitative = SATQ
  )
```

Fit a model as you usually would, and pass it to `apa_parameters`. Here, ACT scores are predicted from SAT Verbal and SAT Quantitative scores:

```{r}
#| label: first-table
fit <- lm(ACT ~ Verbal + Quantitative, data = d_sat)
apa_parameters(fit)
```

In a Quarto or R Markdown document, the result is displayed as an APA-style table. In the console, it prints as a tibble, so you can look at it or change it with dplyr functions before it is displayed. For example, you might want to use `filter` to drop rows or `mutate` to customize the display of a one or more variables.

To customize the table, or to save it to a Word file, pass it to `apa_flextable`, which returns a flextable. Any flextable function can change it further (e.g., `flextable::bold` can selectively bold cells):

```{r}
#| label: first-flextable
apa_parameters(fit) |>
  apa_flextable(font_size = 10, table_width = .6) 
```

# Table Notes

Every table records how it was made, and `apa_note` turns that record into the text of a table note: what the abbreviations stand for, which tests were used, how *p*-values were adjusted, and what the stars mean.

```{r}
#| label: note
apa_parameters(fit, starred = "p") |>
  apa_note()
```

`apa_flextable(note = TRUE)` puts the note below the table:

```{r}
#| label: note-flextable
apa_parameters(fit, starred = "p") |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

When using [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/), put the note in the `apa-note` chunk option instead, as described in the [table notes section of the regression article](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/regression.html#table-notes). Some notes cite the articles that describe a method; `apa7_write_bib` writes their references so that the citations appear in your reference list (see [citations in notes](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/regression.html#citations-in-notes)).

# A Tour of the Table Functions

Each family of tables has an article with examples and options.

| Analysis | Functions | Article |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| Regression (linear, logistic, count, ordinal, multinomial) | `apa_parameters`, `apa_performance`, `apa_performance_comparison`, `apa_collinearity` | [Regression](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/regression.html) |
| Multilevel models (lme4, glmmTMB, nlme) | `apa_parameters`, `apa_performance` | [Multilevel models](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/multilevel.html) |
| ANOVA | `apa_anova` | [ANOVA](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/anova.html) |
| Marginal means, contrasts, simple slopes | `apa_means`, `apa_contrasts`, `apa_slopes` | [Marginal means](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/marginal-means.html) |
| *t* tests, Wilcoxon tests, correlation tests, chi-square tests | `apa_htest` | [Hypothesis tests](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/htest.html) |
| Descriptive statistics ("Table 1") | `apa_descriptives` | [Descriptive statistics](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/descriptives.html) |
| Correlation matrices | `apa_cor` | [Correlations](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/correlations.html) |
| Contingency tables | `apa_chisq` | [Contingency tables](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/chisquare.html) |
| Reliability and item analysis | `apa_reliability` | [Reliability](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/reliability.html) |
| Factor analysis | `apa_loadings`, `apa_factor_cor` | [Factor analysis](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/factor-analysis.html) |
| Structural equation models (lavaan) | `apa_parameters`, `apa_performance`, `apa_loadings` | [Structural equation models](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/lavaan.html) |
| Meta-analysis (metafor) | `apa_parameters`, `apa_performance`, `apa_publication_bias` | [Meta-analysis](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/meta-analysis.html) |
| Any data frame | `apa_flextable` and helpers | [Building tables by hand](https://wjschne.github.io/apa7/articles/summarize.html) |

Here are a few more. A descriptive statistics table, with a column for each group:

```{r}
#| label: tour-descriptives
apa_descriptives(d_sat, by = Gender)
```

A correlation matrix, with means and standard deviations:

```{r}
#| label: tour-cor
apa_cor(d_sat[, c("Age", "ACT", "Verbal", "Quantitative")])
```

A list of nested models gives one table, with the change in *R*^2^:

```{r}
#| label: tour-list
apa_parameters(list(
  lm(ACT ~ Verbal, data = d_sat),
  lm(ACT ~ Verbal + Quantitative, data = d_sat)
))
```

# APA Style Outside of Tables

apa7's formatting functions are useful in text, too, especially in inline R code (e.g., `` `r knitr::inline_expr("apa_p(.0004, inline = TRUE)")` ``).

*p*-values have no leading zero, and very small ones are written as "\<.001" in tables (and "*p* \< .001" in text):

```{r}
#| label: apa-p
apa_p(c(.0004, .0312, .5))
apa_p(.0312, inline = TRUE)
```

`p2stars` converts *p*-values to stars, and `apa_p_star_note` writes the note that explains them:

```{r}
#| label: stars
p2stars(c(.0004, .0312, .5))
apa_p_star_note()
```

`align_chr` rounds numbers, replaces hyphens with true minus signs, and pads the numbers so that they line up on their decimals in a table column. `sci_md` writes very large or very small numbers in scientific notation:

```{r}
#| label: numbers
align_chr(c(2.431, -0.4, -10))
sci_md(c(123251, 0.00045, 12.3))
```

The markdown helpers write italics, bold, subscripts, and superscripts, which apa7 tables and Quarto documents display:

```{r}
#| label: markdown
italic_md("M")
paste0("*R*", superscript_md("2"), subscript_md("adj"))
```

# Defaults

`apa7_defaults` sets options for all tables, such as the rounding accuracy, the font and its size, the line spacing, the label of the intercept, and the width of the page that tables fill (6.5 inches, the text width of letter-size paper with 1-inch margins, unless changed to another width in inches or to a paper size such as `"a4"`):

```{r}
#| label: defaults
#| eval: false
apa7_defaults(accuracy = .001, 
              font_family = "Arial",
              font_size = 11,
              line_spacing = 1,
              intercept_text = "Intercept",
              width_aware_padding = FALSE,
              page_width = "a4", 
              print = "tibble",
              citations = "keys"
              )

# Back to the defaults
apa7_defaults(reset = TRUE)
```

Each of these settings is also an R option

| Argument            | Option                   | Default           |
|:--------------------|:-------------------------|:------------------|
| accuracy            | apa7.accuracy            | .01               |
| font_family         | apa7.font_family         | "Times New Roman" |
| font_size           | apa7.font_size           | 12                |
| line_spacing        | apa7.line_spacing        | 2                 |
| intercept_text      | apa7.intercept_text      | "Constant"        |
| width_aware_padding | apa7.width_aware_padding | TRUE              |
| page_width          | apa7.page_width          | 6.5               |
| landscape_width     | apa7.landscape_width     | NA                |
| column_width        | apa7.column_width        | NA                |
| table_width         | apa7.table_width         | 1                 |
| print               | apa7.print               | "auto"            |
| citations           | apa7.citations           | "auto"            |

For example, to set the default font family:

```{r}
#| label: fontdefault
#| eval: false

options(apa7.font_family = "Arial")
```

# Table Widths

A manuscript can have tables of three widths: the text area of a portrait page, the text area of a landscape page, and one column of a two-column page. Every apa7 function that makes a table has a `table_width` argument that can name any of them:

```{r}
#| label: table-widths
#| eval: false
apa_flextable(apa_parameters(fit), table_width = "page")      # 6.5 in (the default)
apa_flextable(apa_parameters(fit), table_width = "landscape") # 9 in
apa_flextable(apa_parameters(fit), table_width = "column")    # 3.36 in
```

The widths in the comments are for letter-size paper. They follow the `page_width` setting: with `apa7_defaults(page_width = "a4")`, they are 6.27, 9.69, and 3.25 inches. A landscape page's text width is the paper's height less 1-inch margins, and a column's width is that of a column in apaquarto's two-column journal mode (`documentmode: jou`), which has 0.75-inch side margins and a gutter of 4% of the text width between the columns. To set either one yourself, use the `landscape_width` and `column_width` arguments of `apa7_defaults` (in inches).

A table can also be a proportion of one of these widths, or have a width in inches, centimeters, or millimeters:

| `table_width`          | Width                                            |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `1`                    | The default width (the portrait page, unless changed) |
| `.5`                   | Half the default width                           |
| `"page"` or `"portrait"` | The text area of a portrait page              |
| `"landscape"`          | The text area of a landscape page                |
| `"column"`             | One column of a two-column page                  |
| `c(landscape = .8)`    | 80% of the landscape width                       |
| `c(cm = 10)`           | 10 centimeters (also `inches` and `mm`)          |
| `0`                    | Only as wide as the contents                     |

## One Table at a Time

In a Quarto document, the width of one table can be set in its code chunk with the `apa7-width` option, so that a table printed automatically (without `apa_flextable`) gets that width, and no other table is affected:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-landscape
#| apa7-width: landscape
apa_parameters(fit)
```
````

A named number is written as a YAML map (e.g., `#| apa7-width: {landscape: .8}`). In R Markdown, the option is `apa7.width` (e.g., `{r, apa7.width = "landscape"}`). A `table_width` given to a function overrides the chunk option.

## Widths From the Document

You may not need to set any widths at all. When `page_width` and `table_width` are not set with `apa7_defaults`, apa7 reads them from the document being rendered: its `papersize` (e.g., `papersize: a4`) sets the paper, and [apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/)'s `documentmode` sets the margins. In journal mode (`documentmode: jou`), which sets the text in two columns with 0.75-inch margins, every table is as wide as a column unless it asks for another width, and a table in a chunk with `apa-twocolumn: true` spans both columns.

## Two-Column Documents

In a two-column document that is not in apaquarto's journal mode, make the column the default width for every table:

```{r}
#| label: two-column
#| eval: false
apa7_defaults(table_width = "column")
```

Proportions are then proportions of the column (e.g., `table_width = .5` is half a column). A table that spans both columns, which apaquarto makes with the `apa-twocolumn: true` chunk option, is as wide as the page without any other setting.

# Writing a Paper with apaquarto

[apaquarto](https://wjschne.github.io/apaquarto/) is a Quarto extension that formats a whole document in APA style, with the title page, headings, citations, references, and figures and tables in their proper places, and renders it to Word, HTML, PDF, or Typst. `install_apaquarto` installs it in the current project, and `make_apaquarto` opens an app that writes a new document for you:

```{r}
#| label: apaquarto
#| eval: false
install_apaquarto()
make_apaquarto()
```
